title: Foundation-model failure on thin tubular anatomy scales with curvature-to-caliber ratio, not contrast.
problem: Known: promptable segmentation FMs (SAM-family, MedSAM, SAM-Med3D) degrade badly on vessels, airways, and ducts, but the failure is usually attributed vaguely to 'thin structures'.
hypothesis: FM Dice/clDice on tubular structures is predicted primarily by local curvature-to-diameter ratio and branch order, and only weakly by local contrast-to-noise, i.e., failure is geometric-prior-driven, not signal-driven.
why_important: If failure is geometric, more data or contrast enhancement will not fix it; the finding redirects effort toward geometry-aware training/decoding.
why_novel: Failure reports exist, but a controlled regression of error onto per-branch geometric covariates (holding contrast fixed via matched sampling) has not been published to my knowledge.
minimal_experiment: Run 3-4 public FMs zero-shot with box/point prompts on DRIVE, STARE, ATM22 airway, Parse2022 pulmonary vessels; compute per-branch geometry covariates from GT centerlines; fit mixed-effects regression of per-branch recall on curvature/diameter/branch-order/CNR.
main_risk: Geometry and contrast covary in real anatomy; matched-sampling may leave too few branches for significance.
datasets: DRIVE, STARE, CHASE_DB1, ATM22, Parse2022 (all public, registration for challenge sets)
survival_note: Cheap, falsifiable, high information; strong Stage-2 candidate.

title: Quantify the 2D-slice information deficit: which organs are fundamentally ambiguous without 3D context.
problem: Known: many medical FMs operate slice-wise; some structures (adrenals vs veins, bowel loops, esophagus) may be indistinguishable in single slices even for experts.
hypothesis: For a measurable subset of abdominal structures, expert single-slice identification accuracy is itself below 90%, and slice-wise FM error on these structures is bounded by this human single-slice ambiguity rather than model capacity.
why_important: Separates 'FM is weak' from 'the task is ill-posed in 2D'; justifies or refutes the 3D-FM research program organ-by-organ.
why_novel: The 2D-vs-3D debate is argued with aggregate Dice, never with a human single-slice ceiling measurement per structure.
minimal_experiment: Show radiologists isolated single slices from BTCV/AMOS22 and ask them to label structure identity/extent; compare their single-slice accuracy profile against slice-wise FM errors per structure.
main_risk: Recruiting enough expert readers; slice sampling policy strongly affects the ceiling estimate.
compute: Minimal GPU; mostly a small human reader study
survival_note: Human-study logistics are the bottleneck; keep if a clinical collaborator exists.

title: Medical FMs place boundaries at intensity gradients while ground truth encodes functional/anatomic conventions; measure the systematic offset.
problem: Known: natural-image pretraining teaches models that object boundaries coincide with photometric edges; many medical GT boundaries (tumor infiltration margins, organ capsules invisible on CT) do not.
hypothesis: FM boundary error has a consistent signed bias toward the nearest strong intensity gradient, and the magnitude of this bias predicts which organs/lesions FMs fail on across datasets.
why_important: A signed, directional error model is actionable (bias correction, convention-aware evaluation) whereas symmetric distance metrics hide it.
why_novel: Boundary error is nearly always reported as unsigned HD95/ASSD; signed gradient-relative decomposition of FM errors is largely unexplored.
minimal_experiment: For MedSAM/SAM2 outputs on LiTS, KiTS, BraTS: compute signed distance from predicted boundary to GT, correlate the sign/magnitude with local gradient direction and strength; test whether bias direction points toward gradients significantly more than chance.
main_risk: GT itself may be gradient-biased (annotators use edges too), confounding the reference.
survival_note: Strong: cheap, mechanistic, reusable analysis tooling.

title: Foundation models cannot represent absence: hallucinated segmentation of surgically removed or congenitally absent organs.
problem: Known: prompted FMs must return a mask; post-nephrectomy, post-cholecystectomy, and agenesis cases exist in routine data but are rare in curated training sets.
hypothesis: When text- or class-prompted for an absent organ, current medical FMs produce a non-empty, anatomically plausible mask in the majority of cases, and the hallucination rate is not reduced by confidence thresholding at any operating point that preserves sensitivity on present organs.
why_important: Absence handling is a hard safety requirement for deployment (e.g., auto-contouring in radiotherapy) and is invisible to standard benchmarks that only contain present organs.
why_novel: Empty-target evaluation exists for lesions, but a systematic organ-absence stress test for promptable/class-prompted FMs is missing.
minimal_experiment: Mine post-nephrectomy/cholecystectomy cases from public CT collections (e.g., TCIA series, KiTS pre/post cases), prompt VISTA3D/SAT/MedSAM-class models for the absent organ, measure non-empty-mask rate and volume distribution vs matched controls.
main_risk: Curating enough verified absence cases from public data; surgical beds have ambiguous appearance.
datasets: TCIA collections, KiTS (public; absence cases need manual curation)
survival_note: High clinical impact, moderate curation cost; keep.
suspected_published: possibly - empty-prediction handling is discussed in metric papers (Metrics Reloaded line), but organ-absence hallucination audits of FMs appear unpublished

title: Granularity ambiguity is the dominant prompt failure in medical images because nested structures are the norm, not the exception.
problem: Known: a point prompt on a liver tumor is ambiguous between tumor, liver, and abdomen; SAM handles ambiguity with multi-mask output tuned to natural-image object statistics.
hypothesis: The entropy of plausible mask granularities per point prompt is measurably higher in medical images than natural images, and FM multi-mask heads capture the wrong granularity distribution (they miss the clinically intended level in a majority of nested cases).
why_important: Explains a large fraction of interactive-FM failure without invoking domain shift; motivates granularity-aware prompting interfaces.
why_novel: SAM's ambiguity handling is known, but nobody has quantified the granularity distribution mismatch between natural and medical domains.
minimal_experiment: Sample point prompts uniformly inside nested GT structures (tumor-in-organ pairs from LiTS/KiTS/BraTS); enumerate which GT level each SAM/MedSAM multi-mask output matches; compare granularity-hit histograms with COCO/LVIS nested cases.
main_risk: Defining 'plausible granularity levels' objectively; requires datasets with nested labels.
survival_note: Good conceptual payoff; analysis is straightforward.
suspected_published: possibly - SAM-in-medical surveys mention ambiguity; the quantitative granularity-entropy comparison seems open

title: Per-image intensity normalization in FMs destroys the calibrated HU signal that low-contrast organ segmentation depends on.
problem: Known: CT is quantitatively calibrated (Hounsfield units); SAM-style pipelines normalize each image to [0,1] or ImageNet statistics, discarding absolute intensity.
hypothesis: For low-contrast organs (pancreas, adrenal, esophagus), a model given absolute HU features outperforms the same model with per-image normalization by a margin that exceeds the FM-vs-nnU-Net gap, i.e., normalization choice is a first-order cause of FM underperformance on CT.
why_important: A trivial preprocessing decision may explain a chunk of 'domain gap' currently attributed to architecture or data; correcting it is free.
why_novel: Normalization is treated as boilerplate; no controlled study isolates absolute-intensity loss as a failure cause for promptable FMs on CT.
minimal_experiment: Fine-tune identical small decoders on frozen FM features computed from (a) per-image normalized and (b) HU-windowed-but-absolute inputs on BTCV/AMOS pancreas/adrenal; compare against nnU-Net with matched data.
main_risk: Frozen-feature setup may bottleneck both conditions equally, masking the effect.
survival_note: Cheap and decisive either way; keep.

title: FM performance across anatomy is predicted by structure frequency in pretraining corpora, not intrinsic difficulty.
problem: Known: medical FMs report per-organ results, but 'hard organs' are conflated with 'rare-in-training organs'.
hypothesis: Across the ~100 TotalSegmentator classes, corpus frequency (estimated from the published training-set composition of each FM) explains more variance in zero-shot FM Dice than image-derived difficulty covariates (size, contrast, shape complexity).
why_important: If frequency dominates, 'foundation' claims are misleading and targeted data collection beats architectural work for the long tail.
why_novel: Scaling/frequency analyses exist for LLMs and classification; per-structure frequency-vs-difficulty regression for 3D medical seg FMs is missing.
minimal_experiment: Evaluate VISTA3D/SAT/SAM-Med3D on TotalSegmentator test classes; regress per-class Dice on documented training-set class counts and on difficulty covariates; compare explained variance.
main_risk: Training-set composition is only partially documented for some FMs, adding noise to the frequency estimate.
survival_note: Strong; directly informs data strategy for any medical FM effort.
suspected_published: possibly - partial analyses in FM papers' appendices; the systematic regression seems open

title: Pathological deformation breaks FM shape priors: performance conditioned on mass effect, not just lesion presence.
problem: Known: FMs segment normal anatomy well but cases with large masses displacing organs are underrepresented; failure reports are anecdotal.
hypothesis: FM organ-segmentation error grows superlinearly with a quantitative deformation index (displacement of organ centroid from population atlas position), while nnU-Net-style supervised models degrade sublinearly, revealing that FMs rely more heavily on canonical spatial priors.
why_important: Deformed anatomy is exactly where auto-segmentation is clinically needed (surgical/RT planning in tumor patients).
why_novel: Deformation-conditioned evaluation with an explicit atlas-displacement covariate has not been used to compare FM vs supervised model degradation.
minimal_experiment: Register KiTS/LiTS cases to an atlas, compute per-case organ displacement/compression indices, evaluate FMs and nnU-Net on organs adjacent to tumors, fit degradation curves vs deformation index.
main_risk: Registration to atlas is itself unreliable in deformed cases; need robust covariate estimation.
survival_note: Keep; clear clinical framing and falsifiable curve shape claim.

title: Contrast-phase shift hurts CT foundation models more than scanner shift: a controlled two-factor study.
problem: Known: contrast-enhancement phase (non-contrast/arterial/portal-venous) massively changes organ appearance; most robustness studies vary site/scanner instead because phase labels are scarce.
hypothesis: Holding scanner constant, arterial-to-portal-venous phase change causes a larger FM Dice drop on liver/kidney/pancreas than a vendor change at fixed phase; phase is the dominant unmodeled covariate in abdominal CT robustness.
why_important: Determines what metadata must accompany deployment and what augmentation/conditioning actually matters for CT FMs.
why_novel: Phase is usually pooled or ignored; a factorial phase-x-scanner decomposition for FMs is unpublished as far as I know.
minimal_experiment: Use phase-annotated public data (FLARE metadata, TCIA multiphase collections e.g. hepatic multiphase series) to build a 2x2 phase/vendor grid; evaluate 3 FMs; two-way ANOVA on per-case Dice.
main_risk: Public multiphase data with reliable phase and vendor labels is limited; grid may be unbalanced.
datasets: FLARE22/23, TCIA multiphase liver collections (public with registration)
survival_note: Keep; feeds directly into B2 taxonomy work.

title: Ultrasound FM failure is driven by probe/orientation priors, not speckle noise.
problem: Known: FMs do poorly on ultrasound; the standard explanation is speckle statistics, but US training data consists almost exclusively of standard acquisition planes.
hypothesis: FM segmentation on standard planes (apical 4-chamber, standard thyroid views) is substantially better than on off-plane frames of the same anatomy at matched image quality, indicating the deficit is view-prior overfitting rather than noise robustness.
why_important: Redirects US-FM work from denoising/speckle modeling toward view diversity in training data.
why_novel: Plane-vs-off-plane conditioning of FM performance has not been isolated; speckle is assumed to be the culprit without a controlled test.
minimal_experiment: From CAMUS (echo) and TN3K/BUSI (thyroid/breast), plus any cine sweeps, compare FM performance on canonical frames vs adjacent off-canonical frames with matched SNR; additionally add synthetic speckle perturbations to canonical frames as control arm.
main_risk: Public off-plane US with GT is scarce; may need small re-annotation effort.
survival_note: Keep if small annotation budget available.

title: Specular highlights are a spurious cue for polyp segmentation models including FMs: counterfactual highlight removal.
problem: Known: endoscopy images contain strong specular highlights; polyps are often shiny; datasets do not control for this.
hypothesis: Inpainting specular highlights (a physically local, label-preserving intervention) reduces polyp segmentation recall of both specialized models and FMs by a nontrivial margin, demonstrating causal reliance on specularity rather than polyp morphology.
why_important: Specularity depends on light source and processor vendor, so this spurious cue directly undermines cross-hospital transfer of colonoscopy AI.
why_novel: Highlight inpainting is used as preprocessing to help models; using it as a counterfactual probe of cue reliance is a different, unexplored purpose.
minimal_experiment: Detect+inpaint specular regions on Kvasir-SEG/CVC-ClinicDB/PolypGen test sets (classical detection + diffusion inpainting, manually QC'd); measure per-polyp recall change; stratify by polyp type (sessile vs pedunculated).
main_risk: Inpainting artifacts could themselves depress performance; needs sham-inpainting control on non-highlight regions.
survival_note: Strong: causal design with cheap intervention and control.

title: Interactive correction dynamics: click-response oscillation as a fingerprint of FM boundary ambiguity.
problem: Known: interactive FMs are evaluated by Dice-vs-clicks curves; clinicians report frustrating oscillation where fixing one region breaks another.
hypothesis: The frequency of non-monotone Dice trajectories under simulated corrective clicking is a stable model property that (a) differs strongly across FMs at equal 5-click Dice and (b) predicts human editing time better than final Dice.
why_important: Editing time, not final Dice, is the deployment cost; a cheap simulated proxy for it would change how interactive models are selected.
why_novel: Click curves are standard; oscillation statistics and their validation against human editing time are not.
minimal_experiment: Implement standard robot-user clicking on 4 interactive models (SAM2, MedSAM, SAM-Med3D, nnInteractive) over BTCV/BraTS; record per-case Dice trajectories; compute non-monotonicity metrics; small human study (2-3 annotators) to correlate with real editing time.
main_risk: Robot-user policies may not elicit the oscillations humans cause; human study adds cost.
survival_note: Keep; novel evaluation dimension with practical pull.

title: Text-promptable medical segmentation fails systematically on negation, laterality, and clinical abbreviations.
problem: Known: text-prompted models (SAT-style, CLIP-driven) are evaluated on canonical class names; clinical language uses laterality ('left kidney'), negation ('non-enhancing'), and abbreviations ('GB wall').
hypothesis: A structured linguistic perturbation suite (laterality swap, negation insertion, abbreviation substitution, synonym substitution) reveals accuracy drops that are largest for laterality (near-chance left/right selection) and that scale of the text encoder does not fix laterality errors.
why_important: Text prompting is pitched as the clinical interface; if laterality fails, it is unusable and unsafe (wrong-side errors are never-events in medicine).
why_novel: Linguistic robustness suites exist for VQA/NLI; a laterality/negation probe for text-prompted medical segmentation is missing.
minimal_experiment: Build ~40 prompt templates over paired organs in AMOS22/TotalSegmentator; evaluate SAT/BiomedParse-style models; report per-perturbation accuracy and left/right confusion matrices.
main_risk: Few strong open text-prompted 3D models exist; results may date quickly as models improve.
survival_note: Very cheap; do early as a probe paper.
suspected_published: possibly - BiomedParse-adjacent works test synonyms; laterality/negation stress specifically seems open

title: SAM2-style memory tracking fails at polyp re-identification after occlusion in colonoscopy video: characterize the re-entry failure mode.
problem: Known: video FMs track via memory banks; colonoscopy has frequent full occlusions (folds, water, camera withdrawal) after which the same lesion re-enters looking different.
hypothesis: Re-detection recall after full occlusion decays sharply with occlusion duration and viewpoint change, and failure is dominated by appearance-memory staleness rather than detection failure (the lesion is segmentable when prompted fresh).
why_important: Miss-then-reacquire is the clinically critical loop for polyp surveillance; frame-level metrics hide it.
why_novel: Video FM evaluations use VOS-style benchmarks with mild occlusions; a medical occlusion-re-entry stress protocol with the fresh-prompt control is new.
minimal_experiment: On SUN-SEG video sequences, identify occlusion events, run SAM2 tracking vs fresh-prompt-after-occlusion; measure recall gap vs occlusion length/viewpoint delta.
main_risk: Occlusion event labeling is manual; SUN-SEG access requires application.
survival_note: Keep; crisp failure mode with a built-in control condition.

title: Recognition-localization dissociation in FM features: medical structures are linearly identifiable but not linearly localizable.
problem: Known: FM embeddings support strong linear-probe classification of anatomy; segmentation quality with frozen features lags far behind.
hypothesis: Across FM layers, anatomical identity is decodable from mid-layer global features while boundary position is decodable only at low precision from any layer, and this localization deficit (not semantic deficit) accounts for most of the frozen-feature segmentation gap versus fine-tuned models.
why_important: Tells us whether medical FM adaptation should retrain encoders or only add localization-capable decoders; shapes the parameter-efficiency debate with evidence.
why_novel: Layer-wise probing is common in interpretability; a recognition-vs-localization decomposition targeted at the medical frozen-feature gap is not.
minimal_experiment: Probe DINOv2/MedSAM encoders layer-by-layer on BTCV: (a) organ-identity linear probes, (b) boundary-distance regression probes; compare probe ceilings with frozen-feature and fine-tuned segmentation results.
main_risk: Probe capacity choices can bias conclusions; needs careful matched-capacity design.
survival_note: Keep; mechanistic and reusable across FMs.
suspected_published: possibly - dense-probing papers exist for natural images; medical localization-deficit framing seems open

title: End-to-end miss rate of prompt-dependent FMs on small metastases: the detection bottleneck nobody benchmarks.
problem: Known: promptable FMs are evaluated with GT-derived prompts, which presumes a detector; small lesions must first be found.
hypothesis: When prompts come from realistic detectors (or auto-prompting) instead of GT boxes, lesion-level sensitivity of the full pipeline drops most steeply for lesions under ~10 mm, and the pipeline is strictly dominated by end-to-end trained detection-segmentation models at equal compute.
why_important: GT-prompt evaluation systematically overstates clinical utility for metastasis workflows (liver mets, lung nodules, bone lesions).
why_novel: The GT-prompt inflation problem is mentioned in passing in some papers, but a size-stratified end-to-end audit across lesion datasets is missing.
minimal_experiment: On LiTS lesions, MSD lung, and DeepLesion subsets: compare GT-box prompts vs detector-generated prompts vs auto-prompting for MedSAM-class models; report lesion-level FROC by size bin.
main_risk: Detector choice becomes a confounder; must sweep several operating points.
survival_note: Strong; likely to become a citable negative-control benchmark.
suspected_published: possibly - individual papers note prompt-source sensitivity; systematic size-stratified audit seems open

title: Do FM boundaries fall inside the inter-rater band? Multi-rater positioning of foundation-model errors.
problem: Known: single-rater GT makes FM boundary errors look worse or better than they are; multi-rater data (LIDC-IDRI 4 raters, QUBIQ) lets us ask where FM boundaries sit relative to human disagreement.
hypothesis: A substantial fraction of FM 'errors' lie within the inter-rater variability band (thus are not errors in a meaningful sense), but FMs also produce a distinct class of out-of-band errors whose spatial signature (e.g., leakage along gradients) differs qualitatively from any human rater.
why_important: Recalibrates how much of the reported FM-vs-specialist gap is real; defines a principled error taxonomy for regulatory discussion.
why_novel: Multi-rater data is used to evaluate uncertainty models, but rarely to relocate FM error relative to the human disagreement envelope.
minimal_experiment: On LIDC-IDRI and QUBIQ tasks, compute rater-envelope masks; classify FM boundary segments as in-band vs out-of-band; characterize out-of-band error morphology and frequency vs specialized models.
main_risk: Rater envelopes from 3-4 raters underestimate the true plausible band.
survival_note: Keep; cheap and rhetorically powerful.

title: Semantics-versus-boundary error decomposition: FMs delineate well but identify wrongly in intensity-similar lesion classes.
problem: Known: cyst vs solid lesion vs abscess can share boundaries with different clinical meaning; FM evaluations conflate 'wrong region' with 'right region, wrong identity'.
hypothesis: For lesion segmentation tasks with class labels, FM error decomposes with a much larger identity-error share than supervised specialists at matched boundary quality; i.e., FMs have learned generic 'blob delineation' but not medical semantics.
why_important: If true, the fix is semantic supervision, not better decoders; also affects how FM outputs should be consumed downstream (never trust the class).
why_novel: Panoptic-style decomposition (recognition quality vs segmentation quality) is standard in natural images but rarely applied to medical FM audits.
minimal_experiment: On KiTS (cyst vs tumor labels) and BraTS subregions, compute RQ/SQ-style decomposition for FMs vs nnU-Net; compare identity-error shares.
main_risk: Class-labeled lesion datasets are few; conclusions may not generalize beyond kidney/brain.
survival_note: Keep; simple, reuses panoptic machinery.

title: Fine-tuning a medical FM on one target destroys its promptability elsewhere: measure the promptability-retention curve.
problem: Known: labs routinely fine-tune SAM-variants for a single organ/task; the collateral damage to general promptable behavior is unmeasured.
hypothesis: Full fine-tuning on a single organ reduces zero-shot prompted performance on unrelated organs by a large, dose-dependent amount (catastrophic promptability forgetting), while parameter-efficient tuning preserves most of it at small in-task cost - and the retention-vs-gain frontier differs by organ system.
why_important: Institutions want one model, many uses; without retention numbers, fine-tuning decisions are blind.
why_novel: Catastrophic forgetting is classic, but 'promptability' as the retained capability (not class accuracy) is a new measurement target.
minimal_experiment: Fine-tune MedSAM on KiTS kidneys with (full FT / LoRA / decoder-only); before-after prompted evaluation across 20 held-out structures in AMOS22/TotalSegmentator; plot retention curves vs tuning dose.
main_risk: Result may depend heavily on learning-rate details; needs disciplined sweeps.
survival_note: Keep; practically decision-relevant for every hospital ML team.
suspected_published: possibly - PEFT-vs-FT comparisons exist; promptability-retention as the outcome seems open

title: Pathology FMs interpolate magnification but do not extrapolate it: a held-out-magnification generalization test.
problem: Known: WSI pyramids provide discrete magnifications; pathology FMs (UNI/CONCH/Virchow-class) train on mixtures but evaluation never isolates magnification extrapolation.
hypothesis: Segmentation/detection probes on FM features degrade gracefully for magnifications inside the training range but collapse beyond it (both directions), and the collapse is not explained by resolution alone (downsampled in-range images do better than true out-of-range acquisitions).
why_important: Scanners and protocols differ in native magnification; extrapolation failure means silent cross-lab degradation.
why_novel: Scale robustness in pathology is discussed, but a controlled in-range-vs-out-of-range design with the resolution-matched control is not established.
minimal_experiment: Using CAMELYON16/17 and PANDA pyramids: train tumor-region probes at 10x-20x, test at 40x and 2.5x; control arm with synthetic rescaling; compare degradation profiles across 3 pathology FMs.
main_risk: Pyramid levels differ in optical properties (not pure scaling), which is also the point but complicates interpretation.
survival_note: Keep; pathology FM hype needs exactly this kind of audit.

title: Slice-wise FM masks violate 3D shape continuity in ways that predict error without ground truth.
problem: Known: 2D FMs applied slice-wise produce 3D-inconsistent masks; inconsistency is treated as a nuisance to smooth away.
hypothesis: The magnitude of inter-slice inconsistency (surface roughness, component flicker across slices) is a strong unsupervised predictor of true volumetric error at case level (rank correlation > 0.6), enabling label-free failure flagging.
why_important: Deployment needs error detection without GT; a free signal already inside the predictions would be widely usable.
why_novel: Consistency-based quality estimation exists for ensembles/TTA; using intrinsic 3D-inconsistency of slice-wise FMs as the signal has not been validated.
minimal_experiment: Run MedSAM slice-wise on BTCV/AMOS volumes; compute inconsistency indices; correlate with true Dice per case; compare against TTA-variance and confidence baselines.
main_risk: Smooth-but-wrong failures (confident hallucination) evade the signal; must report failure taxonomy of the detector itself.
survival_note: Keep; cheap and immediately useful if it works.

title: FMs hallucinate anatomy inside metal-artifact regions instead of expressing uncertainty: quantify artifact-conditioned hallucination.
problem: Known: hip implants, dental fillings, and spinal hardware create streak artifacts that obliterate signal; models still output masks there.
hypothesis: Within artifact-corrupted voxel regions, FM predictions match atlas-prior expectations (population-average shapes) far above chance while their confidence remains high, demonstrating prior-driven hallucination with miscalibrated certainty.
why_important: Implant patients are common in RT planning; hallucinated contours in artifact zones are a concrete patient-safety issue.
why_novel: Metal artifact reduction is studied for reconstruction; hallucination auditing of segmentation FMs inside artifacts is not.
minimal_experiment: Curate implant cases from TotalSegmentator/VerSe; mask out artifact regions; compare FM predictions there against (a) atlas prediction and (b) GT; measure confidence distributions inside vs outside artifacts.
main_risk: GT inside severe artifacts is itself unreliable; may need CT-MR paired cases for arbitration.
datasets: TotalSegmentator, VerSe (public; implant subset needs curation)
survival_note: Keep; strong safety narrative.

title: Pediatric failure of adult-trained FMs tracks developmental stage, not body size.
problem: Known: FMs trained on adult data do worse on children; the assumed cause is scale, which rescaling should fix but reportedly does not fully.
hypothesis: After optimal isotropic rescaling, residual FM error on pediatric CT/MRI correlates with age-dependent compositional features (ossification centers, thymus prominence, organ proportion shifts) rather than with patient size, falsifying the 'just resize' assumption.
why_important: Pediatric imaging is chronically data-poor; knowing whether the gap is geometric or compositional determines whether synthesis/augmentation can close it.
why_novel: Pediatric evaluations exist but do not dissociate size from developmental composition using rescaling controls.
minimal_experiment: On pediatric-containing public sets (e.g., TCIA pediatric collections, FeTA for fetal brain), evaluate FMs with and without size normalization; regress residual error on age with size partialled out.
main_risk: Public pediatric segmentation GT is scarce; statistical power limited.
survival_note: Marginal unless pediatric data access improves; park if blocked.

title: In-context (one-example) medical segmentation fails across acquisition context: build the context-transfer matrix.
problem: Known: visual in-context learning (SegGPT-style, universal prompting) segments a target given one annotated reference; medical references rarely match target phase/sequence/scanner.
hypothesis: In-context performance is dominated by reference-target acquisition mismatch (phase, sequence, vendor) rather than anatomical mismatch: a same-acquisition different-patient reference beats a same-patient different-acquisition reference.
why_important: Determines how reference libraries for in-context clinical tools must be organized (by acquisition, not by anatomy).
why_novel: In-context segmentation papers ablate reference choice superficially; a factorial acquisition-vs-anatomy transfer matrix is new.
minimal_experiment: Using multi-sequence BraTS and multiphase liver data, run in-context models across a reference-target grid (same/different patient x same/different sequence); report the full transfer matrix.
main_risk: Current in-context models may be uniformly weak on medical data, flattening the matrix.
survival_note: Keep; matrix result is informative whatever it shows.

title: Prompt-jitter ensembles as calibrated uncertainty: does prompt sensitivity predict FM error?
problem: Known: FM output varies under small prompt perturbations; this instability is reported as a flaw but never exploited or validated as an uncertainty signal.
hypothesis: Variance of masks under systematic prompt jitter is better correlated with true error than MC-dropout or TTA variance for promptable FMs, because it probes exactly the decision boundary the interface exposes; calibration of jitter-derived confidence transfers across organs (falsifiable via reliability diagrams).
why_important: Free, architecture-agnostic uncertainty for the dominant interactive paradigm; useful for triage and QA.
why_novel: Prompt sensitivity has been measured; its validation as calibrated, transferable uncertainty against alternatives has not.
minimal_experiment: On BTCV/BraTS, generate 16-point jitter ensembles per case for MedSAM/SAM-Med3D; compute error-vs-variance correlation, reliability diagrams, and cross-organ calibration transfer; baselines: TTA, dropout.
main_risk: Jitter scale is a free parameter; conclusions must be robust across scales.
survival_note: Strong; borderline method-flavored but fundamentally a measurement-validity study.
suspected_published: possibly - prompt-ensemble uncertainty appears in workshop papers; rigorous calibration-transfer validation seems open

title: Shape-complexity-conditioned failure: FMs regress complex organs toward blobs; quantify the simplification bias.
problem: Known: pancreas tail, adrenal limbs, and cortical folds are frequently truncated or rounded off by FMs; 'hard organ' explanations do not separate complexity from size/contrast.
hypothesis: Predicted-shape complexity (e.g., surface-area-to-volume, curvature energy) is systematically lower than GT complexity for FMs, and the deficit grows with GT complexity - a shape-shrinkage law analogous to regression-to-the-mean.
why_important: A quantified simplification bias would explain a family of errors and motivate complexity-preserving evaluation (current metrics reward blobs).
why_novel: Regression-to-mean-shape is folklore; measuring it as a law across organs and models, and linking it to metric incentives, is new.
minimal_experiment: Compute complexity statistics of GT vs predictions for 5 models across TotalSegmentator classes; fit shrinkage slopes; test whether Dice-optimal post-processing increases shrinkage (metric-incentive link).
main_risk: Complexity metrics sensitive to resolution/annotation smoothness; needs careful normalization.
survival_note: Strong; links to evaluation-weakness cluster B11.

title: A registration-based atlas baseline beats zero-shot FMs on low-contrast organs: an honest negative-control benchmark.
problem: Known: classical multi-atlas segmentation was SOTA pre-2015 and is ignored in FM comparisons; FMs are compared only against each other and nnU-Net.
hypothesis: For low-contrast, shape-stable organs (pancreas body, esophagus, adrenals), a modern but classical multi-atlas pipeline outperforms zero-shot medical FMs, exposing that FM zero-shot claims for these organs are below a 2013-era bar.
why_important: Field-level sanity check; prevents wasted effort and inflated claims; atlas methods also provide interpretable failure modes.
why_novel: Nobody wants to run this comparison; that is precisely the gap. Honest negative results here are scarce.
minimal_experiment: Implement ANTs-based multi-atlas with label fusion on BTCV/AMOS (20 atlases); compare against zero-shot VISTA3D/SAT/MedSAM on the same test split, organ-stratified.
main_risk: Atlas pipelines need tuning; a badly tuned baseline would invert the intended honesty.
survival_note: Keep; cheap infrastructure, high field-hygiene value.

title: Within-patient temporal shift: FMs fail on post-treatment anatomy (fibrosis, clips, cavities) more than cross-patient shift predicts.
problem: Known: robustness is studied across patients/sites; longitudinal within-patient change after surgery/radiation is a distinct shift axis nobody benchmarks.
hypothesis: For the same patient, FM performance on post-treatment scans drops more than the cross-patient variability band, and errors concentrate at treatment-altered interfaces (resection margins, fibrotic bands) rather than being spatially uniform.
why_important: Follow-up imaging is the highest-volume clinical use case (response assessment); models tuned on treatment-naive data silently degrade exactly where monitoring matters.
why_novel: Longitudinal within-patient robustness of segmentation FMs is essentially unstudied; public longitudinal GT exists in pockets.
minimal_experiment: Use longitudinal series in BraTS follow-up sets / TCIA post-treatment glioma and HNSCC collections; compare FM error pre vs post treatment within patient; map error concentration relative to treated regions.
main_risk: Longitudinal GT quality varies; treatment metadata sometimes missing.
datasets: BraTS post-treatment sets, TCIA longitudinal collections (public)
survival_note: Keep; clinically central and under-benchmarked.

title: Boundary-convention regression: FMs trained on mixed datasets learn an average annotation convention that matches no dataset.
problem: Known: 'aorta' includes/excludes branches, 'tumor' includes/excludes edema depending on dataset; FMs train on unions of datasets with silently conflicting conventions.
hypothesis: On structures with known convention conflicts, FM predictions sit between conventions (measurably bimodal-averaged boundaries) and per-dataset evaluation penalizes them in opposite directions - i.e., part of the reported FM gap is convention mismatch, not perceptual failure.
why_important: Reframes some 'errors' as label-space disagreements; motivates convention-conditioning rather than more data.
why_novel: Convention conflicts are known anecdotally; measuring convention-averaging behavior in trained FMs is new.
minimal_experiment: Pick 5 structures with documented convention differences across BTCV/AMOS/TotalSegmentator; measure signed boundary offsets of FM predictions toward each convention; test bimodality/averaging against single-dataset supervised models.
main_risk: Requires careful documentation of conventions; some differences are undocumented and must be measured first.
survival_note: Strong; bridges to dataset-failure cluster B12.

title: The prompt bottleneck in dense instance regimes: promptable FM cost scales linearly with instance count in nuclei/gland segmentation.
problem: Known: pathology requires segmenting thousands of nuclei per image; per-instance prompting makes FM inference cost and error scale with instance count.
hypothesis: There exists a measurable instance-density threshold beyond which promptable-FM pipelines (any prompting policy) are Pareto-dominated by promptless dense models in both accuracy and cost, and this threshold is low enough (order 10^2 instances) to exclude FMs from most pathology dense tasks.
why_important: Draws a principled applicability boundary for the promptable paradigm instead of case-by-case anecdotes.
why_novel: Cost-accuracy scaling of prompting versus instance density has not been formalized or measured.
minimal_experiment: On MoNuSeg/PanNuke/GlaS, sweep instance density; compare prompted FM pipelines (grid/auto prompts) vs HoVer-Net-class models on accuracy-vs-FLOPs curves; locate crossover.
main_risk: Auto-prompting improvements could move the threshold; report as threshold-vs-prompt-policy family.
survival_note: Keep; produces a decision rule, not just a complaint.

title: Diffuse, non-blob disease breaks the FM objectness prior: measure the objectness penalty on infiltrative and multifocal targets.
problem: Known: FMs inherit an 'object' prior from natural images; ground-glass opacity, peritoneal carcinomatosis, and infiltrative gliomas are textures/regions, not objects.
hypothesis: FM performance drop from blob-like to diffuse targets (within the same modality and organ system) exceeds the drop attributable to intensity contrast, and scales with a quantifiable 'objectness' score of the GT mask (compactness, boundary gradient alignment).
why_important: Diffuse disease drives major clinical decisions (ILD extent, peritoneal cancer index); knowing FMs are structurally unsuited redirects tooling.
why_novel: Objectness as a measured covariate of FM failure, with contrast controlled, has not been isolated.
minimal_experiment: Assemble target spectrum: LiTS focal lesions -> BraTS infiltrative regions -> ILD/GGO masks (public COVID-19 CT seg sets) -> carcinomatosis if available; regress FM error on objectness score with contrast covariates.
main_risk: Cross-dataset confounds along the spectrum; needs within-dataset gradients too.
datasets: LiTS, BraTS, COVID-19 CT segmentation sets, MSD (public)
survival_note: Strong; complements 0386 shape-shrinkage.

title: Tree-truncation depth: FMs and supervised models stop segmenting airway/vessel trees at characteristic branch generations; measure and compare the truncation law.
problem: Known: airway and vessel segmentations systematically miss distal branches; completeness is reported as a single number hiding where trees get cut.
hypothesis: Each model family has a characteristic branch-generation survival curve (probability a generation-k branch is captured), the curve shape is stable across patients, and FMs truncate 1-2 generations earlier than specialized topology-aware models at equal Dice.
why_important: Distal completeness determines clinical utility (bronchoscopy planning, vessel analysis); survival-curve reporting would change how tree segmentation is compared.
why_novel: Generation-stratified 'survival analysis' framing of tree completeness is new as an evaluation primitive.
minimal_experiment: On ATM22 and Parse2022, extract GT branch generations; compute capture probability per generation for FMs vs specialized baselines; fit parametric survival curves.
main_risk: GT itself truncates distal branches; ceiling effects must be modeled.
survival_note: Keep; also feeds evaluation cluster B11.

title: Empty-slice behavior: what promptable FMs do when prompted on slices with no target present.
problem: Known: in 3D workflows, prompts propagate to slices where the organ has ended; promptable models are trained to always return a mask.
hypothesis: On slices immediately beyond an organ's true extent, FMs return non-empty masks at high rates with confidence indistinguishable from true-positive slices, making organ-extent errors (first/last slice) a dominant, structured error source in volumetric measurements.
why_important: Organ volume and craniocaudal extent drive clinical measures; extent errors are systematic, not random, so they bias measurements.
why_novel: Slice-extent failure of prompt propagation has not been isolated as a measurement-bias problem.
minimal_experiment: On BTCV/AMOS, propagate prompts 1-5 slices past GT extent; measure non-empty rates, confidence, and induced volume bias; compare across propagation strategies.
main_risk: Somewhat narrow; could be folded into a larger extent-error study.
survival_note: Cheap probe; merge candidate with 0364/0381.

title: Cross-modality prompt-embedding transfer: do spatial prompts mean the same thing to an FM in CT and MR?
problem: Known: FMs claim modality generality; whether the prompt-conditioned decoding behaves consistently across modalities for the same anatomy is untested.
hypothesis: For registered CT-MR pairs of the same patient (CHAOS), identical prompts produce masks whose disagreement across modality substantially exceeds intra-modality test-retest disagreement, revealing modality-specific prompt semantics rather than anatomy-grounded behavior.
why_important: Cross-modality consistency is a necessary condition for claiming anatomical understanding; a cheap consistency test can benchmark it without new labels.
why_novel: Registered-pair prompt-consistency testing is an unused evaluation design for medical FMs.
minimal_experiment: Use CHAOS CT+MR same-patient data; register; apply identical prompt sets; measure cross-modality mask agreement vs within-modality jitter agreement; per-organ breakdown.
main_risk: Registration error inflates disagreement; need deformable registration QC and error propagation.
datasets: CHAOS (public); AMOS22 CT/MR unpaired as secondary
survival_note: Keep; label-free evaluation designs are valuable.

title: Anisotropy stress test: FM failure under thick-slice CT is driven by resampling policy, not information loss.
problem: Known: FMs are evaluated mostly on thin-slice research data; clinical archives are 3-5mm thick-slice; pipelines resample anisotropic volumes differently.
hypothesis: At fixed slice thickness, the choice of resampling policy (interpolation kernel, target spacing, 2D-vs-3D handling) changes FM Dice by more than the difference between 1.5mm and 5mm native acquisitions handled optimally - i.e., the community's 'thick-slice problem' is substantially a pipeline artifact.
why_important: If pipeline dominates, harmonizing resampling recovers performance for free across archives; if not, thick-slice data genuinely needs new models.
why_novel: Resampling is boilerplate nobody ablates systematically for FMs; the thickness-vs-pipeline decomposition is unmeasured.
minimal_experiment: Take thin-slice TotalSegmentator volumes; synthesize thick-slice versions (proper slab averaging); factorial evaluation over resampling policies x thicknesses for 3 FMs; variance decomposition.
main_risk: Synthetic thick slices approximate but do not equal native acquisitions; validate on a small native thick-slice set.
survival_note: Strong; unglamorous but likely high-yield.

title: Rare-orientation blindness: prone, decubitus, and arms-down scans as a cheap out-of-pose stress suite for medical FMs.
problem: Known: training corpora are dominated by supine arms-up CT; prone rectal protocols, decubitus chest, and trauma scans violate pose priors.
hypothesis: FM error on pose-variant scans exceeds supine error by a margin that persists after test-time reorientation to canonical pose, indicating the models encode pose-correlated context (gravity-dependent organ shift, table position) rather than orientation alone.
why_important: Pose variants are routine in specific clinical pathways; the reorientation-resistant component of failure is scientifically interesting (gravity-induced anatomy change is a real covariate).
why_novel: Orientation augmentation is standard; the residual-after-reorientation decomposition on real pose-variant scans is not.
minimal_experiment: Curate prone/decubitus series from TCIA; evaluate FMs raw and after rigid reorientation; compare residual error against supine controls matched by protocol.
main_risk: GT for pose-variant scans mostly absent; needs limited expert annotation (~30 cases).
survival_note: Keep if annotation budget exists; otherwise park.

title: Test-retest reproducibility of medical FMs on same-day repeat scans: noise floor of the measurement instrument.
problem: Known: clinical use treats segmentation-derived measures (volume, diameter) as measurements, but model test-retest variability on same-patient repeat acquisitions is almost never reported.
hypothesis: FM test-retest variability on same-day repeat scans exceeds both scan-rescan physical variability and specialized-model variability, and importantly is organ-dependent in ways uncorrelated with Dice - i.e., accuracy rankings do not predict reproducibility rankings.
why_important: For longitudinal monitoring, reproducibility matters more than accuracy; if rankings decouple, the field is selecting models on the wrong axis.
why_novel: Test-retest analysis is standard in radiomics but essentially absent from FM segmentation evaluation.
minimal_experiment: Use public test-retest collections (RIDER lung CT test-retest, traveling-subject MRI sets); run FMs on both scans; report per-organ volume repeatability coefficients vs supervised baselines.
main_risk: Few public test-retest datasets with relevant anatomy; sample sizes small.
datasets: RIDER Lung CT (TCIA), traveling-subject MRI (e.g., SRPBS), OASIS repeats (public)
survival_note: Strong; measurement-science framing is underused in segmentation.

title: Does interactive FM correction actually converge to expert consensus, or to a model-specific attractor?
problem: Known: interactive FMs are assumed to reach any desired mask given enough corrections; anecdotally they resist certain boundaries.
hypothesis: Under exhaustive simulated correction (clicks until saturation), each FM converges to a mask family with systematic residual deviation from multi-rater consensus (a model attractor), and the attractor deviation is larger where the model's prior conflicts with GT (e.g., gradient-following vs convention boundaries).
why_important: If attractors exist, human-in-the-loop cannot fully fix FM bias - a fundamental limit for the correction paradigm used in clinical products.
why_novel: Saturation-limit analysis of interactive segmentation (what is reachable at all) is unstudied; everyone reports few-click regimes.
minimal_experiment: On LIDC-IDRI/QUBIQ multi-rater tasks, run corrective clicking to saturation (e.g., 50+ clicks with optimal placement); measure residual distance to consensus and its spatial structure across models.
main_risk: Saturation behavior depends on click simulator; use several policies including adversarially optimal.
survival_note: Strong; theoretical limit with practical stakes.

title: Which FM pretraining signal transfers to contrast-free segmentation: probing whether models exploit anatomical position encoding.
problem: Known: some organs are segmentable largely from position (spleen is where the spleen is); it is unknown how much FM medical performance is positional lookup versus appearance analysis.
hypothesis: Ablating appearance (replacing organ interior with matched noise while keeping surroundings) degrades FM segmentation far less than expected for organs with stable positions, quantifying a large positional-lookup share that inflates benchmark scores yet fails under anatomical variation.
why_important: Explains simultaneous benchmark success and clinical fragility; positional shortcut share is a new model characteristic worth reporting.
why_novel: Occlusion probing is standard in interpretability; using it to decompose medical seg performance into positional vs appearance shares is not.
minimal_experiment: On BTCV/AMOS, replace organ interiors with intensity-matched noise; measure FM performance retention per organ; correlate retention with organ positional variance across population.
main_risk: Noise infill introduces edge artifacts; must use boundary-preserving infill and sham controls.
survival_note: Strong; cheap causal probe, connects to shortcut cluster B12.

title: Stress-testing FM robustness to reconstruction algorithm: iterative and deep-learning-reconstructed CT as an invisible domain.
problem: Known: hospitals increasingly use vendor deep-learning reconstruction (DLR); public segmentation datasets are dominated by FBP/iterative recon; recon algorithm is rarely recorded in ML papers.
hypothesis: Segmentation FMs show a measurable, organ-dependent performance and boundary-bias shift on DLR images relative to FBP reconstructions of the same raw data, and the shift direction is consistent with DLR's noise-texture smoothing (boundary contraction on low-contrast organs).
why_important: DLR adoption is rapid and silent; if it shifts segmentation output, longitudinal consistency of measurements breaks without anyone noticing.
why_novel: DLR effects are studied for radiomics features, not for segmentation FMs; the paired-reconstruction design isolates the factor perfectly.
minimal_experiment: Use paired-reconstruction public data (LDCT-and-Projection-data on TCIA allows re-reconstruction; some vendors provide paired sets); run FMs on both recon versions; paired per-organ analysis of Dice and signed boundary shift.
main_risk: Access to true paired DLR/FBP data is limited; simulation-based DLR proxies weaken the claim.
compute: 1 GPU, ~2 GPU-days (+ recon compute if re-reconstructing)
datasets: LDCT-and-Projection-data (TCIA), Mayo low-dose CT (public with registration)
survival_note: Keep; radiomics literature suggests effect is real, segmentation version open.
